planting.note: Direct-sow scarified or soaked seed in spring once soil has warmed, at the sunny margin of a pond, rain garden, or chenier swale where the trailing vine can climb a fence or shrub or sprawl as a groundcover.

directions: Sow seed directly in spring after the soil has warmed, scarifying or soaking the hard-coated seed to speed germination; this twining, trailing legume thrives along the moist, slightly brackish edges of chenier swales, marsh-fringe ditches, and pond margins where cheniers meet the surrounding prairie-marsh mosaic. Give it a fence, shrub, or trellis to scramble over, or let it sprawl as a groundcover at the sunny edge of a rain garden. Clusters of small yellow pea-like flowers appear through summer and fall and reliably draw skipper butterflies, while the foliage and seed are valuable forage for waterfowl and other wildlife. In zone 9a it behaves as a root-hardy perennial, dying back after frost and resprouting from the crown the following spring.

planting.note: Set divisions or rooted rhizome pieces in spring into consistently wet, humus-rich soil at a pond, ditch, or rain-garden margin, and keep the soil saturated through establishment.

directions: Plant divisions or rhizome segments in spring into consistently wet to saturated, humus-rich soil at the margin of a pond, ditch, or rain garden, the kind of seasonally flooded swale that collects behind chenier ridges in the Louisiana and upper Texas coastal prairie-marsh mosaic. This slender, rhizomatous perennial spreads gradually into loose colonies and bears small, widely spaced tubular white to pale lavender flowers on open spikes from summer into fall. It tolerates both standing water and the periodic drying of marsh-edge soils better than many wetland perennials, which makes it a useful, low-maintenance choice for stabilizing soft, muddy banks. Give it full sun and avoid letting it dry out for extended stretches.

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring into consistently moist to wet soil in full sun at a marsh, ditch, or pond margin; thin seedlings to give the vigorous summer growth room to spread.

directions: Direct-sow in spring into moist to wet soil in full sun; this fast-growing perennial colonizes the fresh-to-brackish marsh edges, drainage ditches, and pond margins typical of the chenier plain, often forming loose stands several feet tall alongside bulltongue and maidencane. Four-petaled, bright yellow flowers roughly an inch across open continuously from early summer through fall, followed by the distinctive eight-ribbed seed capsules that give the species its name. It tolerates both standing water and brief dry spells once established, and in mild Gulf Coast winters it persists as a root-hardy perennial, cut back hard by frost and regrowing from the base in spring. Site it where its somewhat sprawling growth has room to spread without crowding smaller companions.

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring into saturated, saline to brackish mud or sand in a constructed marsh bed or tidal container feature, and keep it consistently flooded with brackish water.

directions: Direct-sow seed in spring into saline to brackish, saturated mud or sand at the fringe of a marsh or tidal pool feature, the same low, flooded flats where this jointed, fleshy-stemmed succulent forms dense perennial mats along the chenier plain's marsh edges. Unlike the more familiar annual glassworts grown as a quick salad crop, this species persists for years, spreading low mounds of bright green, coral-like stems that often flush red or amber in fall. It needs full sun and consistently wet, salty to brackish soil, which makes it best suited to a built salt-marsh bed, bog garden, or large container flooded periodically with diluted seawater rather than an ordinary border. Young tips can be harvested sparingly for a crisp, salty garnish, as with other glassworts.
